newsitem.title: FRANCE: France gets US explanations on Africa criticisms.
newsitem.headline: France gets US explanations on Africa criticisms.

text.p: France asked for and received an explanation from Washington after reports the U.S. ambassador to Zaire made stinging criticism of Paris's policy in Africa, the Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday.
Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux told reporters the explanation came from State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns but declined to give details or say if France was satisfied.

Doutriaux was answering reporters' questions about an interview given last week to Zairean newspapers by the U.S. envoy to Kinshasa, Daniel Simpson, who reportedly said: "France is no longer capable of imposing its will in Africa."
He was quoted as saying: "Neo-colonialism is no longer tolerated. The French attitude no longer reflects the reality of the situation."
Burns told reporters on Monday: "I don't know what the full text of his (Simpson's) remarks are, I haven't seen them. I don't know if he has been taken out of context...
Paris and Washington have partly been at odds over Zaire ever since Rwandan-backed rebels invaded the east of the country several weeks ago.

Paris, which supports Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and backed Rwanda's former regime, spearheaded international moves to aid refugees caught in the Zairean turmoil and accused Washington of foot-dragging.
An international force including French and American troops was since created on paper but it has yet to get off the ground.
The exchange between Paris and Washington over Africa is the latest in a series.

The most bitter incident was before last month's U.S. presidential election when a French minister, commenting on an African visit by Secretary of State Warren Christopher, said the U.S. administration became interested in Africa solely at election-time in order to win the votes of Afro-Americans.

France, a former colonial power, has long considered French-speaking West and Central Africa a preserve and smarted at what it believes are U.S., and possibly British efforts, to take its place in the area.
